title: Detection of Code Repositories
summary: This strategy detects the search for victim owned code repositories, ATT&CK sub technique T1593.003, which is reconnaissance activity that happens before any intrusion. An adversary queries public code hosting platforms and public code search services for the organisation name, product names, internal hostnames or email domains, looking for accidentally committed credentials, internal documentation and application details. The telemetry is not on the endpoint at all: it comes from web proxy or secure web gateway logs that record the request host and full uniform resource locator, from recursive domain name system resolver logs, and where available from continuous integration and code hosting audit records for repository enumeration. Detection works by combining an internal indicator from the request, such as the company domain or a private product name, with a code hosting or code search destination, then ageing that against the organisation's own automated scanning and the developers who legitimately browse those sites every day. The strategy fails because most of this traffic is encrypted and shared with ordinary developer browsing, and because a determined adversary can query from infrastructure that never touches the corporate network.

beginner.definition: Attackers often look for your company on public code websites before they attack. They hope to find a password left in a shared project, or a note about how your systems are built. This detection looks for searches that combine your company name with a code hosting website. The search itself is not an attack, but it is an early warning.
beginner.whyItMatters: Reconnaissance is cheap and quiet. It also decides where the real attack will land. A developer may have committed a key or a database password into a public project. That finding is worth more to an attacker than any exploit. Early warning gives your team time to remove the exposure. It also lets you watch the person who found it. Without this detection, the first sign of trouble is usually the intrusion itself.
howItWorks: Your secure web gateway writes a log line for each web request. It records the site name and the full address that was requested.
The rule keeps requests going to code hosting and code search services.
It then looks inside the requested address for an internal marker, such as your company domain or a private product name.
It removes the company's own automated scanners and known developer accounts so they do not create noise.
Requests from an unusual user agent, a server address or a single source making many similar queries are kept.
What is left is raised at a low level, as a lead for the threat intelligence team to review.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman writing in a door log. At midnight, a stranger walks along the street outside. They read the company name plate and the signs on the loading bay. They never touch the door. The watchman still writes a line. A stranger was reading the signs at this hour. Weeks later, the building is broken into. The log now gives the police a starting point. Searching public code sites is that stranger on the pavement. This detection is the line in the door log.
takeaways: Reconnaissance produces no damage, but it is the earliest useful warning you can get.
You must combine an internal name with a code hosting site, or the rule will fire on normal developer browsing.
Act on the lead by checking what is public, not only by watching the person who searched.

objectives: Explain the role of open repository reconnaissance in the early stages of an intrusion
Identify the telemetry that can show a search for your organisation on code hosting services
Combine an internal indicator with a code hosting destination to build a meaningful rule
Separate the organisation's own scanning and normal developer activity from external reconnaissance
Describe what an unintended secret disclosure in a public repository means for response
Use reconnaissance alerts to trigger exposure review rather than only network blocking
dataSources: Secure web gateway or forward proxy logs containing request host, full uniform resource locator, user agent and source address
Recursive domain name system resolver logs recording lookups of code hosting and public code search domains
Code hosting platform audit records for repository search, clone and fork events on organisation owned repositories
Continuous integration and build platform access logs showing unauthenticated or external browsing of project pages
Secret scanning alerts from the source control platform indicating committed credentials in public or shared projects
logic: The detection joins a destination that is a code hosting or public code search service with a request element that names the organisation, such as the corporate email domain, a registered product name, an internal project name or a hostname suffix. The fields to correlate are the requested host, the full uniform resource locator including query parameters, the user agent, the authenticated account if any, and the source address. The malicious case is an unauthenticated or unknown user agent, a source address outside the corporate ranges, or a burst of near identical queries that walk through product and domain names in sequence. The benign case is a developer with an authenticated account browsing their own organisation's repositories, an automated dependency scanner, or a marketing team checking public mentions. Volume and novelty matter more than the single request, so the alert should present the query text, the actor and a count over the day.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Search For Organisation On Public Code Hosting Service
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection_service:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'github.com/search'
#       - 'gitlab.com/search'
#       - 'searchcode.com'
#       - 'sourcegraph.com'
#   selection_org_indicator:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'acme-corp'
#       - 'acmecorp.com'
#       - 'project-atlas'
#   filter_developers:
#     authenticated: 'true'
#   condition: selection_service and selection_org_indicator and not filter_developers
# level: low
falsePositives: Software developers searching public code hosting sites for open source examples and library usage during normal work
Automated dependency, licence and software composition analysis tools that query public repositories and code search application programming interfaces
Recruitment and marketing staff checking public profiles and public repositories that mention the company name
The organisation's own security or threat intelligence team performing authorised exposure assessments against its public footprint
tuningNotes: Correlate the search with an authenticated account and a corporate source address first, because nearly all legitimate traffic to these services comes from known developers on managed devices during working hours. Build a filter for your own exposure scanning ranges and for the user agents of dependency and licence scanners, and re-check it every quarter since those tools change. Scope the first release to queries that contain your email domain or a private product name, which sharply reduces volume, and leave generic company name searches at an even lower level. Narrowing this far costs you visibility into an adversary who searches abbreviations or a recently acquired brand, so maintain a synonym list of organisation names and review it with the communications team twice a year.
